claim: RELION-4.0 presents a new approach for macromolecular structure determination from multiple particles in electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) data sets.
source: We present a new approach for macromolecular structure determination from multiple particles in electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) data sets.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main contribution of the work.

claim: Existing subtomogram averaging approaches are based on 3D data models.
source: Whereas existing subtomogram averaging approaches are based on 3D data models, we propose to optimise a regularised likelihood target that approximates a function of the 2D experimental images.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge contrasting with the proposed approach.

claim: RELION-4.0 optimizes a regularised likelihood target that approximates a function of the 2D experimental images.
source: Whereas existing subtomogram averaging approaches are based on 3D data models, we propose to optimise a regularised likelihood target that approximates a function of the 2D experimental images.
evidence: This is the core methodological claim of the paper.

claim: RELION-4.0 includes approaches analogous to Bayesian polishing and CTF refinement from single-particle analysis.
source: In addition, analogous to Bayesian polishing and contrast transfer function (CTF) refinement in single-particle analysis, we describe the approaches that exploit the increased signal-to-noise ratio in the averaged structure to optimise tilt-series alignments, beam-induced motions of the particles throughout the tilt-series acquisition, defoci of the individual particles, as well as higher-order optical aberrations of the microscope.
evidence: This describes the methods implemented in the software.

claim: RELION-4.0 approaches allow structure determination from cryo-ET data to resolutions sufficient for de novo atomic modelling.
source: We illustrate for three applications that our approaches allow structure determination from cryo-ET data to resolutions sufficient for de novo atomic modelling.
evidence: This is the main result claim supported by the three test cases presented.

claim: Electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) has allowed 3D imaging of an increasing number of biological macromolecules at resolutions sufficient for de novo atomic modelling in recent years.
source: In recent years, electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM) has allowed the 3D imaging of an increasing number of biological macromolecules at resolutions sufficient for de novo atomic modelling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Advances in detector technology originally drove the development of cryo-EM for high-resolution imaging.
source: This development, originally driven by advances in detector technology, was further facilitated by novel, robust image processing algorithms.
evidence: This is stated as historical context for the field.

claim: Novel, robust image processing algorithms have facilitated cryo-EM development.
source: This development, originally driven by advances in detector technology, was further facilitated by novel, robust image processing algorithms.
evidence: This is stated as historical context for the field.

claim: In single-particle analysis, images of multiple copies of isolated macromolecular complexes suspended in random orientations in vitreous water are combined in a 3D reconstruction.
source: In single-particle analysis, images of multiple copies of isolated macromolecular complexes, or particles, that are suspended in random orientations in a thin layer of vitreous water are combined in a 3D reconstruction.
evidence: This describes the standard single-particle analysis approach.

claim: Many aspects of single-particle analysis workflows can be performed with minimal human supervision.
source: Nowadays, many aspects of single-particle analysis workflows can be performed with only minimal human supervision, for example, the detection, extraction, and initial classification of particles in the images (Zivanov et al., 2018; Bepler et al., 2019; Wagner et al., 2019), 3D reconstruction (Zivanov et al., 2018; Punjani et al., 2017), as well as refinement of the optical parameters (Zivanov et al., 2018; Zivanov et al., 2020; Punjani et al., 2017; Tegunov et al., 2021) and per-particle tracking of electron beam-induced motion (Zheng et al., 2017; Zivanov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published methods.

claim: Detection, extraction, and initial classification of particles in images can be performed with minimal human supervision.
source: Nowadays, many aspects of single-particle analysis workflows can be performed with only minimal human supervision, for example, the detection, extraction, and initial classification of particles in the images (Zivanov et al., 2018; Bepler et al., 2019; Wagner et al., 2019), 3D reconstruction (Zivanov et al., 2018; Punjani et al., 2017), as well as refinement of the optical parameters (Zivanov et al., 2018; Zivanov et al., 2020; Punjani et al., 2017; Tegunov et al., 2021) and per-particle tracking of electron beam-induced motion (Zheng et al., 2017; Zivanov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published methods.

claim: Modern single-particle analysis methods are built on solid statistical foundations that require few tunable parameters.
source: Many of the algorithms that underlie these modern methods are built on solid statistical foundations that require few tunable parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of modern methods.

claim: Statistical foundations decrease the need for operator expertise in single-particle analysis.
source: This decreases the need for operator expertise and provides objectivity, as well as robustness, in obtaining optimal structures.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the statistical approach.

claim: Single-particle approach is limited to investigating isolated protein complexes that are purified to relative homogeneity.
source: The single-particle approach is, however, limited to investigating isolated protein complexes that are purified to relative homogeneity.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of the single-particle approach.

claim: Electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) can be used to examine protein complexes in their crowded physiological environment.
source: To examine these complexes in their crowded physiological environment, electron cryo-tomography (cryo-ET) may be used instead.
evidence: This is stated as the advantage of cryo-ET over single-particle analysis.

claim: In the tomographic approach, the sample is tilted multiple times during image acquisition, yielding a tilt series of images from which a 3D tomogram can be computed.
source: In the tomographic approach, the sample is tilted multiple times during image acquisition, yielding a so-called tilt series of images from which a 3D tomogram can be computed.
evidence: This describes the basic tomographic data acquisition process.

claim: Repeated occurrences of particles in tomograms can be aligned and averaged to obtain higher-resolution reconstructions through subtomogram averaging.
source: In the same manner as single-particle analysis, repeated occurrences of particles in those tomograms can then be aligned and averaged to obtain higher-resolution reconstructions. This process is referred to as subtomogram averaging.
evidence: This describes the subtomogram averaging process.

claim: Labs use many different tools for subtomogram averaging.
source: Unlike the field of single-particle analysis, labs use many different tools for subtomogram averaging (e.g. Kremer et al., 1996; Nickell et al., 2005; Heumann et al., 2011; Castaño-Díez et al., 2012; Hrabe et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013; Galaz-Montoya et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019; Jiménez de la Morena et al., 2022) and many of the tools used require considerable levels of expertise from the operator, often in order to tune parameters that arise from heuristics in the underlying algorithms.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to different software tools.

claim: Many subtomogram averaging tools require considerable levels of expertise from the operator.
source: Unlike the field of single-particle analysis, labs use many different tools for subtomogram averaging (e.g. Kremer et al., 1996; Nickell et al., 2005; Heumann et al., 2011; Castaño-Díez et al., 2012; Hrabe et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2013; Galaz-Montoya et al., 2016; Sanchez et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2019; Jiménez de la Morena et al., 2022) and many of the tools used require considerable levels of expertise from the operator, often in order to tune parameters that arise from heuristics in the underlying algorithms.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of existing subtomogram averaging tools.

claim: Subtomogram averaging faces several unique challenges compared to single-particle analysis.
source: Compared to single-particle analysis, subtomogram averaging faces several unique challenges.
evidence: This introduces the discussion of challenges in subtomogram averaging.

claim: Subtomogram averaging algorithms must estimate the position and orientation of each particle as well as consider the geometry of the tilt series.
source: In addition to estimating the position and orientation of each particle, the algorithm also has to consider the geometry of the tilt series.
evidence: This describes the computational challenges of subtomogram averaging.

claim: Subtomogram averaging typically involves preprocessing steps including CTF estimation and tilt series alignment, followed by tomogram reconstruction.
source: Typically, this is solved through a set of preprocessing steps that include estimation of contrast transfer function (CTF) parameters and alignment of the tilt series, followed by the reconstruction of, often inconveniently large, tomograms for the entire field of view.
evidence: This describes the typical workflow for subtomogram averaging.

claim: The separation between tomogram reconstruction and subtomogram averaging can lead to an accumulation of errors.
source: The separation between tomogram reconstruction and subtomogram averaging can lead to an accumulation of errors, because errors in the CTF estimation or tilt-series alignments are hard to correct.
evidence: This is stated as a problem with the traditional workflow.

claim: Subtomograms contain empty regions in Fourier space called the missing wedge because the sample cannot be rotated 180° within the microscope.
source: In addition, because the sample cannot be rotated 180° within the microscope, the subtomograms contain empty regions in Fourier space, the so-called missing wedge, which are difficult to deal with in subtomogram averaging (e.g. see Schmid and Booth, 2008; Förster et al., 2008; Bartesaghi et al., 2008; Frank et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a known problem in subtomogram averaging with citations.

claim: A fundamental problem with subtomogram averaging is that it transforms the original 2D image data into 3D subtomograms, which are then used as a substitute for experimental data in the alignment algorithm.
source: A fundamental problem with subtomogram averaging as described above is that it transforms the original 2D image data into 3D subtomograms, which are then used as a substitute for experimental data in the alignment algorithm.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental problem with traditional subtomogram averaging.

claim: RELION-2 introduced the concept of a 3D CTF to describe the transfer of information from the 2D images to the subtomograms.
source: RELION-2 introduced the concept of a 3D CTF to describe the transfer of information from the 2D images to the subtomograms, which dealt to some extent with the missing wedge and the loss of information through interpolations in the reconstruction algorithm (Bharat and Scheres, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a previous contribution with citation.

claim: The 3D CTF approach does not deal correctly with the lower resolution regions of Fourier space, where information from different tilt images overlaps.
source: A drawback of the 3D CTF approach is that it does not deal correctly with the lower resolution regions of Fourier space, where information from different tilt images overlaps.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the 3D CTF approach.

claim: Formulating the optimisation target function directly as a function of the actual 2D images measured in the microscope is a statistically more attractive approach.
source: A statistically more attractive approach would be to formulate the optimisation target function directly as a function of the actual 2D images that are measured in the microscope.
evidence: This is stated as the motivation for the 2D approach.

claim: Constrained single-particle cryo-ET processes individually boxed particles from tilt-series images as in single-particle analysis, but keeps their relative orientations fixed.
source: This has been proposed in an approach called constrained single-particle cryo-ET (Bartesaghi et al., 2012), where individually boxed particles from the tilt-series images are processed as in single-particle analysis, but their relative orientations are kept fixed.
evidence: This describes a previous approach with citation.

claim: A similar approach to constrained single-particle cryo-ET was implemented in the program emClarity.
source: A similar approach was also implemented in the program emClarity (Himes and Zhang, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the emClarity program.

claim: The program M introduced new optimisation approaches that compare reference projections against the 2D particle images to deal with unknowns in the relative orientations of particles and their CTFs.
source: To deal with unknowns in the relative orientations of the particles from the tilt-series images, as well as their CTFs, the program M recently introduced new optimisation approaches that compare reference projections against the 2D particle images (Tegunov et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the M program approach with citation.

claim: M relies on RELION for alignment and classification of 3D subtomograms that are recalculated from the optimised parameters in M.
source: M relies on RELION for alignment and classification of 3D subtomograms that are recalculated from the optimised parameters in M.
evidence: This describes the relationship between M and RELION.

claim: The iterative approach of M and RELION allows subtomogram averaging to resolutions that approach those observed for single-particle analysis, even for particles in complex cellular environments.
source: Nevertheless, this iterative approach allows subtomogram averaging to resolutions that approach those observed for single-particle analysis, even for particles in complex cellular environments (Tegunov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to the M program paper.

claim: RELION-4.0 uses pseudo-subtomograms: explicitly constructed sets of 3D data arrays that contain sums of CTF pre-multiplied 2D tilt-series images.
source: In order to do so at acceptable computational and implementation costs, we have altered the main refinement program in RELION-4.0 to work with so-called pseudo-subtomograms: explicitly constructed sets of 3D data arrays that contain sums of CTF pre-multiplied 2D tilt-series images, together with auxiliary arrays that contain the corresponding sum of squared CTFs and how often each 3D voxel has been observed.
evidence: This describes the key technical innovation of RELION-4.0.

claim: Pseudo-subtomograms no longer aim to represent the actual scattering potential of the underlying particles.
source: Pseudo-subtomograms no longer aim to represent the actual scattering potential of the underlying particles, in the way that conventional subtomograms would.
evidence: This describes a key difference between pseudo-subtomograms and conventional subtomograms.

claim: Evaluation of the pseudo-subtomograms by RELION-4.0 approximates the likelihood of observing a hypothetical particle in the images of the entire tilt series, given the current model.
source: Evaluation of the pseudo-subtomograms by RELION-4.0 approximates the likelihood of observing a hypothetical particle in the images of the entire tilt series, given the current model.
evidence: This describes what the pseudo-subtomogram approach achieves.

claim: Many proteins are organised in imperfect 2D arrays inside tomograms, for example, inside membranes or as part of capsid-like structures.
source: Many proteins are organised in imperfect 2D arrays inside the tomograms, for example, inside membranes or as part of capsid-like structures.
evidence: This is stated as a common biological observation.

claim: Individual protein molecules inside 2D arrays exhibit limited rotational freedom with respect to the surface normal of the array, although they may be able to rotate freely around that normal.
source: Often, the individual protein molecules inside these arrays exhibit limited rotational freedom with respect to the surface normal of the array, although they may be able to rotate freely around that normal.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of proteins in 2D arrays.

claim: Knowledge about limited rotational freedom is often exploited in subtomogram averaging approaches through local orientational searches.
source: This knowledge is often exploited in subtomogram averaging approaches through local orientational searches, for example, see Förster et al., 2005.
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous approach.

claim: Local orientational searches accelerate refinement and make it possible to solve more challenging structures.
source: This not only accelerates the refinement, as fewer orientations need to be evaluated, it also makes it possible to solve more challenging structures because fewer solutions are allowed.
evidence: This is stated as the benefit of local orientational searches.

claim: RELION implements local orientational searches as Gaussian priors on the Cartesian translations and on the three Euler angles that describe rotations.
source: In RELION, local orientational searches are implemented as Gaussian priors on the Cartesian translations and on the three Euler angles that describe rotations (Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This describes the implementation in RELION with citation.

claim: The coordinate system of the pseudo-subtomograms can be chosen arbitrarily.
source: One advantage of using pseudo-subtomogram alignment is that the coordinate system of the pseudo-subtomograms themselves can be chosen arbitrarily.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the pseudo-subtomogram approach.

claim: By default, pseudo-subtomograms are created in the same orientation as the tomogram.
source: By default, pseudo-subtomograms are created in the same orientation as the tomogram, but the user can choose to orient them in a more meaningful way.
evidence: This describes the default behavior of the software.

claim: Tilt-series refinement procedures do not require pseudo-subtomograms, but are performed by comparing projections of the density maps directly with the pixels of 2D boxes extracted from the tilt-series images.
source: These procedures do not require pseudo-subtomograms, but are performed by comparing projections of the density maps directly with the (Fourier) pixels of 2D boxes that are extracted from the tilt-series images, with a sufficient size to hold the CTF-delocalised signal.
evidence: This describes the tilt-series refinement approach.

claim: Tilt-series properties that can be refined fall into two broad categories: optical and geometrical.
source: The tilt-series properties that can be refined fall into two broad categories: optical and geometrical.
evidence: This categorizes the refinement procedures.

claim: Optical refinement concerns the different parameters of the CTF.
source: The optical refinement concerns the different parameters of the CTF, while the geometrical refinement aims to optimise the alignment of the tilt series, as well as the beam-induced motion of the individual particles.
evidence: This describes what optical refinement addresses.

claim: Geometrical refinement aims to optimise the alignment of the tilt series and the beam-induced motion of the individual particles.
source: The optical refinement concerns the different parameters of the CTF, while the geometrical refinement aims to optimise the alignment of the tilt series, as well as the beam-induced motion of the individual particles.
evidence: This describes what geometrical refinement addresses.

claim: The optical and geometrical refinement algorithms in RELION-4.0 are closely related to the corresponding single-particle algorithms in RELION: optical-aberration refinement and Bayesian polishing.
source: Both sets of algorithms are closely related to the corresponding single-particle algorithms in RELION: optical-aberration refinement (Zivanov et al., 2018; Zivanov et al., 2020) and Bayesian polishing (Zivanov et al., 2019), respectively.
evidence: This is stated with citations to the single-particle methods.

claim: CTF refinement for tomographic data in RELION-4.0 includes optimisation of scale factors that model frequency-dependent radiation damage, defocus, astigmatism, and higher-order symmetrical and antisymmetrical aberrations.
source: CTF refinement for tomographic data in RELION-4.0 includes optimisation of scale factors that model frequency-dependent radiation damage, defocus, astigmatism, and higher-order symmetrical and antisymmetrical aberrations.
evidence: This describes the CTF refinement capabilities.

claim: Individual particles within a field of view are at distinct defoci in the tilt-series images, but their relative defoci are known from the geometry of the tilt series and the known 3D positions of the particles in the tomogram.
source: Although individual particles within a field of view are at distinct defoci in the tilt-series images, their relative defoci are known from the geometry of the tilt series and the known 3D positions of the particles in the tomogram.
evidence: This describes a property of tomographic data that is exploited in the method.

claim: Defocus estimation can be performed efficiently in a single pass, considering all particles in a tilt-series image simultaneously.
source: Therefore, one can efficiently perform defocus estimation in a single pass, considering all particles in a tilt-series image simultaneously.
evidence: This describes an efficiency gain in the method.

claim: Higher-order aberrations are often only a limiting factor at relatively high spatial frequencies.
source: Because the higher-order aberrations are often only a limiting factor at relatively high spatial frequencies, a large number of particles are needed to estimate them reliably.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of higher-order aberrations.

claim: Higher-order aberrations would optimally be estimated globally over the entire data set for cases that yield high-resolution averages.
source: Optimally, higher-order aberrations would thus be estimated globally, over the entire data set, and only for cases that yield high-resolution averages.
evidence: This is stated as a recommendation for when to estimate higher-order aberrations.

claim: Third-order antisymmetrical aberrations (trefoil and axial coma) are typically the most important higher-order aberrations.
source: Typically, the third-order antisymmetrical aberrations are the most important ones, that is, trefoil and axial coma, which can both be caused by a tilted beam.
evidence: This is stated as typical behavior of aberrations.

claim: The resolution gains from higher-order aberration correction depend on the microscope (mis)alignment.
source: The resolution gains that these optimisations will yield depend on the microscope (mis)alignment.
evidence: This is stated as a factor affecting the benefit of aberration correction.

claim: Higher-order aberration correction will probably be most useful for reconstructions that extend beyond 3 Å resolution, provided alignment has been performed reasonably well.
source: Provided alignment has been performed reasonably well, higher-order aberration correction will probably be most useful for reconstructions that extend beyond 3 Å resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction about when aberration correction is useful.

claim: The geometric alignment in RELION-4.0 includes both rigid rotational and translational re-alignment of the tilt-series images, as well as the modelling of beam-induced motion of individual particles throughout the tilt series.
source: The geometric alignment includes both (rigid) rotational and translational re-alignment of the tilt-series images, as well as the modelling of beam-induced motion of individual particles throughout the tilt series.
evidence: This describes the geometric alignment capabilities.

claim: RELION-4.0 neglects rotations of the particles in beam-induced motion modeling and only models beam-induced translations.
source: For the latter, we neglect rotations of the particles, and only model beam-induced translations.
evidence: This describes a simplification in the method.

claim: The workflow was tested on the cryo-ET data set used to determine the structure of the immature capsid lattice and spacer peptide 1 (CA-SP1) regions of the Gag polyprotein from HIV-1.
source: We tested the workflow above on the cryo-ET data set that was used to determine the structure of the immature capsid lattice and spacer peptide 1 (CA-SP1) regions of the Gag polyprotein from human immunodeficiency virus 1 (HIV-1) (Schur et al., 2016) (EMPIAR-10164).
evidence: This describes the first test case with citation.

claim: The same subset of five tomograms from the HIV-1 data set was used to assess the NovaCTF, emClarity, and Warp programs.
source: We used the same subset of five tomograms that were also used to assess the NovaCTF (Turoňová et al., 2017), emClarity (Himes and Zhang, 2018), and Warp (Tegunov and Cramer, 2019) programs.
evidence: This describes the data used for comparison with citations.

claim: NovaCTF reported a resolution of 3.9 Å for the HIV-1 immature capsid using 3D CTF correction.
source: Introducing 3D CTF correction, and using the alignment parameters from the original analysis by Schur et al., NovaCTF reported a resolution of 3.9 Å (Turoňová et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a result from NovaCTF with citation.

claim: The Warp program introduced local and global motion correction in the tilt-series images, as well as optimisation of CTF parameters.
source: The Warp program introduced local and global motion correction in the tilt-series images, as well as optimisation of CTF parameters.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of Warp.

claim: The combination of Warp and subtomogram alignment and averaging in RELION-3 led to a resolution of 3.8 Å for the HIV-1 immature capsid.
source: The combination of Warp and subtomogram alignment and averaging in RELION-3 led to a resolution of 3.8 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from Warp and RELION-3.

claim: A recent application of emClarity led to a reconstruction of the HIV-1 immature capsid to 3.3 Å resolution.
source: A recent application of emClarity led to a reconstruction to 3.3 Å resolution (Ni et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as a result from emClarity with citation.

claim: RELION-4.0 used 12,910 particles from the five tomograms subset of the HIV-1 data set.
source: We used 12,910 particles from the five tomograms subset, reconstructed an initial reference map using the original published particle alignment, and filtered it to 5 Å.
evidence: This describes the data used in the RELION-4.0 analysis.

claim: A first alignment in 3D auto-refine, followed by averaging of the initial pseudo-subtomograms, led to a resolution of 3.6 Å for the HIV-1 immature capsid.
source: A first alignment in 3D auto-refine, followed by averaging of the initial pseudo-subtomograms, led to a resolution of 3.6 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the initial RELION-4.0 processing.

claim: CTF refinement to optimise the defoci of all particles improved the resolution of the HIV-1 immature capsid only marginally.
source: We first applied CTF refinement to optimise the defoci of all particles. This improved the resolution only marginally.
evidence: This is stated as a result from CTF refinement.

claim: Optimisation of the tilt-series geometry, including modelling local particle motion, improved the resolution of the HIV-1 immature capsid to 3.5 Å.
source: Subsequent optimisation of the tilt-series geometry, including modelling local particle motion, improved the resolution to 3.5 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from geometric refinement.

claim: Realignment of newly generated pseudo-subtomograms led to a resolution of 3.4 Å for the HIV-1 immature capsid.
source: Finally, realignment of newly generated pseudo-subtomograms led to a resolution of 3.4 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from realignment.

claim: A second cycle of pseudo-subtomogram improvement and realignment provided 3.3 Å resolution for the HIV-1 immature capsid.
source: A second cycle of these three steps provided 3.3 Å, while a third cycle converged to 3.2 Å (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a result from iterative refinement.

claim: A third cycle of pseudo-subtomogram improvement and realignment converged to 3.2 Å resolution for the HIV-1 immature capsid.
source: A second cycle of these three steps provided 3.3 Å, while a third cycle converged to 3.2 Å (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a result from iterative refinement with reference to a figure.

claim: Analysis of the complete HIV-1 data set generated a structure at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: Analysis of the complete data set generated a structure at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is the same resolution obtained using the M and RELION-3 workflow (Tegunov et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and is likely limited by flexibility and asymmetry in the CA hexamer.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the full data set analysis with reference to figures.

claim: The 3.0 Å resolution obtained for the HIV-1 immature capsid is the same resolution obtained using the M and RELION-3 workflow.
source: Analysis of the complete data set generated a structure at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is the same resolution obtained using the M and RELION-3 workflow (Tegunov et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and is likely limited by flexibility and asymmetry in the CA hexamer.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with citation.

claim: The 3.0 Å resolution for the HIV-1 immature capsid is likely limited by flexibility and asymmetry in the CA hexamer.
source: Analysis of the complete data set generated a structure at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is the same resolution obtained using the M and RELION-3 workflow (Tegunov et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and is likely limited by flexibility and asymmetry in the CA hexamer.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the resolution limit.

claim: The workflow was applied to thin cellular appendages of C. crescentus bacteria known as stalks, which have previously been imaged using cryo-ET.
source: We also applied our approach to thin cellular appendages of C. crescentus bacteria known as stalks, which have previously been imaged using cryo-ET (Bharat et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the second test case with citation.

claim: The cell body and cell stalks of C. crescentus cells are covered by a nearly hexagonal, paracrystalline array known as the surface layer (S-layer).
source: The cell body and cell stalks of C. crescentus cells are covered by a nearly hexagonal, paracrystalline array known as the surface layer (S-layer) (Smit et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation.

claim: The structure of the S-layer was solved using a combination of X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM single-particle analysis, and subtomogram averaging.
source: The structure of the S-layer was solved using a combination of X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM single-particle analysis, and subtomogram averaging, revealing how the S-layer is attached to bacterial cells by an abundant glycolipid called lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Bharat et al., 2017; von Kügelgen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citations.

claim: The S-layer is attached to bacterial cells by lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: The structure of the S-layer was solved using a combination of X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM single-particle analysis, and subtomogram averaging, revealing how the S-layer is attached to bacterial cells by an abundant glycolipid called lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Bharat et al., 2017; von Kügelgen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work with citations.

claim: Previous cryo-ET of the S-layer using 110 tilt series collected with a dose-symmetric scheme yielded 51,866 hexamers of the S-layer.
source: Previously, cryo-ET of the S-layer, using 110 tilt series collected with a dose-symmetric scheme, yielded 51,866 hexamers of the S-layer.
evidence: This describes previous work on the S-layer.

claim: A 7.4 Å reconstruction of the S-layer was obtained using a constrained cross-correlation approach implemented in the AV3 MATLAB suite.
source: This study used a subtomogram averaging approach that is based on a constrained cross-correlation approach implemented in the AV3 MATLAB suite (Förster and Hegerl, 2007), and which was specifically optimised for the analysis of macromolecules arranged in a lattice (Wan et al., 2017). A 7.4 Å reconstruction of the S-layer was obtained, in which alpha-helices were resolved (Bharat et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes previous work with citations.

claim: Application of NovaCTF improved the S-layer reconstruction to 4.8 Å resolution, in which large amino acid residue side chains were resolved.
source: This reconstruction was improved by application of NovaCTF (Turoňová et al., 2017), leading to a 4.8 Å reconstruction, in which large amino acid residue side chains were resolved (von Kügelgen et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes previous work with citations.

claim: Density for an LPS molecule was observed near the putative LPS-binding residues of the S-layer in the 4.8 Å reconstruction, in agreement with a cryo-EM single-particle structure of an in vitro reconstituted complex.
source: Moreover, density for an LPS molecule was observed near the putative LPS-binding residues of the S-layer, in agreement with a cryo-EM single-particle structure of an in vitro reconstituted coplex (von Kügelgen et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a finding from previous work with citation.

claim: Multiple cycles of pseudo-subtomogram generation and refinement led to a 5.6 Å reconstruction of the S-layer hexamer.
source: These parameters were imported into RELION-4.0, followed by multiple cycles of pseudo-subtomogram generation and refinement, analogous to the immature HIV-1 data set described above, leading to a 5.6 Å reconstruction of the S-layer hexamer (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is stated as a result from RELION-4.0 processing with reference to a figure.

claim: Focused refinement with a mask around the central pore of the S-layer improved the resolution to 4.4 Å.
source: Next, we defined a mask around the central pore of the S-layer, corresponding to the inner domain bound to LPS, to perform focused refinements. Another cycle of pseudo-subtomogram reconstruction, CTF refinement, and refinement within the new mask improved the resolution to 4.4 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from focused refinement.

claim: Accounting for per-particle motions increased the resolution of the central pore of the S-layer to 4.0 Å, and the inner domain to 3.7 Å.
source: Accounting for per-particle motions with additional cycles of pseudo-subtomogram improvements and refinements increased the resolution of the central pore to 4.0 Å, and the inner domain of the S-layer to 3.7 Å.
evidence: This is stated as a result from per-particle motion correction.

claim: 3D classification without alignments identified a subset of 42,990 subtomograms that gave a 3.5 Å resolution reconstruction of the inner S-layer.
source: Further 3D classification without alignments identified a subset of 42,990 subtomograms that gave a 3.5 Å resolution reconstruction of the inner S-layer.
evidence: This is stated as a result from 3D classification.

claim: The 3.5 Å S-layer map is in excellent agreement with the single-particle structure of the in vitro reconstituted complex, including the LPS binding site.
source: The 3.5 Å map is in excellent agreement with the single-particle structure of the in vitro reconstituted complex, including the LPS binding site (von Kügelgen et al., 2020; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous work with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Divalent metal ions, known to be tightly bound to the inner S-layer, are resolved in the 3.5 Å map.
source: Furthermore, divalent metal ions, known to be tightly bound to the inner S-layer (Matthew, 2021), are resolved (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: A second LPS binding site was observed at lower isosurface contour levels in the S-layer map.
source: Surprisingly, at lower isosurface contour levels, we also observed a second LPS binding site (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: This is stated as a new finding with reference to figures.

claim: The size and shape of the second LPS binding site density agree with the structure of the LPS O-antigen.
source: The size and shape of this density agree with the structure of the LPS O-antigen, illustrating how improved subtomogram averaging in RELION-4.0 can help uncover new biology.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the density.

claim: The workflow was applied to the Saccharomyces cerevisiae coat protein complex II (COPII).
source: Finally, we applied our approach to the Saccharomyces cerevisiae coat protein complex II (COPII), which mediates the transport of newly synthesised proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus as part of the secretory pathway.
evidence: This describes the third test case.

claim: COPII mediates the transport of newly synthesised proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus as part of the secretory pathway.
source: Finally, we applied our approach to the Saccharomyces cerevisiae coat protein complex II (COPII), which mediates the transport of newly synthesised proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) to the Golgi apparatus as part of the secretory pathway.
evidence: This is stated as background information about COPII.

claim: COPII is formed by five proteins that assemble sequentially on the ER membrane to induce remodelling of the bilayer into coated carriers.
source: COPII is formed by five proteins that assemble sequentially on the ER membrane to induce remodelling of the bilayer into coated carriers in a process known as COPII budding, while simultaneously selectively recruiting cargo into these budding membrane carriers.
evidence: This is stated as background information about COPII.

claim: COPII budding can be reconstituted in vitro from purified proteins and artificial membranes, to form small, spherical vesicles, or long, straight tubes.
source: COPII budding can be reconstituted in vitro from purified proteins and artificial membranes, to form small, spherical vesicles, or long, straight tubes.
evidence: This is stated as background information about COPII.

claim: Cryo-ET has previously been used to visualise the architecture of COPII on reconstituted tubules.
source: Cryo-ET has previously been used to visualise the architecture of COPII on reconstituted tubules (Hutchings et al., 2018; Hutchings et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citations.

claim: The COPII coat assembles into two concentric layers; the inner layer forms a pseudo helical lattice.
source: The coat assembles into two concentric layers; the inner layer forms a pseudo helical lattice, which has previously been solved to 4.6 Å resolution using Dynamo-based subtomogram averaging protocols (Castaño-Díez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation.

claim: The inner layer of the COPII coat has previously been solved to 4.6 Å resolution using Dynamo-based subtomogram averaging protocols.
source: The coat assembles into two concentric layers; the inner layer forms a pseudo helical lattice, which has previously been solved to 4.6 Å resolution using Dynamo-based subtomogram averaging protocols (Castaño-Díez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation.

claim: A first 3D refinement of the unbinned COPII data set gave a map at 4.4 Å resolution.
source: A first 3D refinement of the unbinned data set gave a map at 4.4 Å resolution, which was further improved to 4.2 Å and 4.0 Å by tilt-series frame alignment and CTF refinement, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a result from RELION-4.0 processing.

claim: Tilt-series frame alignment improved the COPII map to 4.2 Å resolution.
source: A first 3D refinement of the unbinned data set gave a map at 4.4 Å resolution, which was further improved to 4.2 Å and 4.0 Å by tilt-series frame alignment and CTF refinement, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a result from frame alignment.

claim: CTF refinement improved the COPII map to 4.0 Å resolution.
source: A first 3D refinement of the unbinned data set gave a map at 4.4 Å resolution, which was further improved to 4.2 Å and 4.0 Å by tilt-series frame alignment and CTF refinement, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a result from CTF refinement.

claim: Two further rounds of 3D refinement, followed by tilt-series frame alignment and CTF refinement, yielded a final COPII map with a resolution of 3.8 Å.
source: Two further rounds of 3D refinement, followed by tilt-series frame alignment and CTF refinement, yielded a final map with a resolution of 3.8 Å (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a result from iterative refinement with reference to a figure.

claim: At 3.8 Å resolution, most side chains are visible in the COPII map, enabling building and refinement of an atomic model.
source: At this resolution, most side chains are visible in the map, enabling us to build and refine an atomic model.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the resolution achieved.

claim: The problem of averaging over multiple identical particles in tomographic tilt series is formulated in an empirical Bayesian framework based on a statistical model that approximates one for two-dimensional experimental data.
source: We formulate the problem of averaging over multiple identical particles in tomographic tilt series in an empirical Bayesian framework that is based on a statistical model that approximates one for two-dimensional experimental data.
evidence: This summarizes the methodological approach.

claim: The Bayesian framework has proven effective in reducing the number of tunable parameters and in obtaining high-quality reconstructions from single-particle data.
source: The Bayesian framework has proven effective in reducing the number of tunable parameters and in obtaining high-quality reconstructions from single-particle data (Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to support the choice of framework.

claim: The two-dimensional data model describes the experimental images better than alternative approaches that use 3D reconstructed subtomograms as an intermediate.
source: The two-dimensional data model describes the experimental images better than alternative approaches that use 3D reconstructed subtomograms as an intermediate.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the 2D approach.

claim: The need for missing wedge correction arises from the observation that the experimental images were acquired, incompletely, in three dimensions.
source: One example of a problem with the intermediate 3D data model is the need for missing wedge correction, which arises from the observation that the experimental images were acquired, incompletely, in three dimensions.
evidence: This explains the origin of the missing wedge problem.

claim: Artefacts related to suboptimal missing wedge correction may affect both alignment and classification of particles.
source: Artefacts related to suboptimal missing wedge correction may affect both alignment and classification of particles.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of missing wedge correction.

claim: By using an approximation to the 2D data model, missing wedge correction is no longer required.
source: By using an approximation to the 2D data model, missing wedge correction is no longer required.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the 2D approach.

claim: The problem approaches that of single-particle analysis when using the 2D data model, where projections from different orientations and of different structural states are sorted out simultaneously.
source: Instead, the problem approaches that of single-particle analysis, where projections from different orientations and of different structural states are sorted out simultaneously.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of using the 2D approach.

claim: Likelihood optimisation techniques have been highly successful in tackling the problem of sorting projections from different orientations and structural states in single-particle analysis, provided the 3D Fourier transform of the distinct classes is fully sampled through the orientation distribution of the raw particles.
source: Provided the 3D Fourier transform of the distinct classes is fully sampled through the orientation distribution of the raw particles, likelihood optimisation techniques have been highly successful in tackling this problem in single-particle analysis (Scheres et al., 2007; Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the approach.

claim: The implementation in RELION-4.0 does not use stacks of 2D projection images as input for the refinement program that performs alignment and classification.
source: In practice, the implementation in RELION-4.0 does not use stacks of 2D projection images as input for the refinement program that performs alignment and classification.
evidence: This describes the implementation choice.

claim: The use of 3D pseudo-subtomograms allowed reusing existing code for subtomogram averaging in RELION.
source: The use of 3D pseudo-subtomograms allowed reusing existing code for subtomogram averaging in RELION, while input stacks of 2D images would have required significant software development efforts.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using pseudo-subtomograms.

claim: A true 2D version of the code might be implemented in the future, which would be more efficient in terms of processing time and disk storage requirements.
source: Nevertheless, in the future we might still choose to implement a true 2D version of the code, which would be more efficient, both in terms of processing time and disk storage requirements.
evidence: This is stated as a potential future development.

claim: In cases where the number of tilt images is small in comparison to the box size, fewer Fourier pixels need to be examined in a stack of 2D images than in a pseudo-subtomogram, with a corresponding decrease in processing time.
source: In cases where the number of tilt images is small in comparison to the box size, fewer Fourier pixels need to be examined in a stack of 2D images than in a pseudo-subtomogram, with a corresponding decrease in processing time.
evidence: This explains when a 2D approach would be more efficient.

claim: The likelihood calculation from the 3D pseudo-subtomogram approach requires separate storage of the accumulated squares of the CTFs and the corresponding multiplicity terms.
source: Moreover, the likelihood calculation from the 3D pseudo-subtomogram approach requires separate storage of the accumulated squares of the CTFs, and the corresponding multiplicity terms.
evidence: This describes a storage requirement of the pseudo-subtomogram approach.

claim: In the 2D approach, only the 2D images need to be stored, as CTF parameters can be calculated on-the-fly and there is no need for a multiplicity term.
source: In contrast, in the 2D approach, only the 2D images need to be stored, as CTF parameters can be calculated on-the-fly and there is no need for a multiplicity term, giving a corresponding decrease in storage requirements.
evidence: This explains the storage advantage of a 2D approach.

claim: If tilt series were collected with very fine angular increments or in a continuous manner, the current pseudo-subtomogram implementation may still be preferable.
source: However, if one were to collect tilt series with very fine angular increments or in a continuous manner (Chreifi et al., 2019), then the current implementation may still be preferable.
evidence: This is stated as a condition where the current approach is preferable with citation.

claim: The implementations in RELION-4.0 follow those previously implemented for single-particle analysis, where CTF refinement is used for re-estimation of the tilt-series images CTFs.
source: The implementations in RELION-4.0 again follow those previously implemented for single-particle analysis, where CTF refinement is used for re-estimation of the tilt-series images CTFs, and algorithms akin to Bayesian polishing are used to re-estimate the tilt-series alignment, as well as the movement of individual particles throughout the tilt-series acquisition process.
evidence: This describes the relationship to single-particle methods.

claim: Algorithms akin to Bayesian polishing are used to re-estimate the tilt-series alignment and the movement of individual particles throughout the tilt-series acquisition process.
source: The implementations in RELION-4.0 again follow those previously implemented for single-particle analysis, where CTF refinement is used for re-estimation of the tilt-series images CTFs, and algorithms akin to Bayesian polishing are used to re-estimate the tilt-series alignment, as well as the movement of individual particles throughout the tilt-series acquisition process.
evidence: This describes the geometric refinement approach.

claim: Better tilt-series parameters will allow better pseudo-subtomograms.
source: As better tilt-series parameters will allow better pseudo-subtomograms, particle alignment and classification are iterated with the optimisation of the tilt-series parameters.
evidence: This explains the rationale for iterative refinement.

claim: Particle alignment and classification are iterated with the optimisation of the tilt-series parameters.
source: As better tilt-series parameters will allow better pseudo-subtomograms, particle alignment and classification are iterated with the optimisation of the tilt-series parameters.
evidence: This describes the iterative workflow.

claim: Similar tilt-series and CTF optimisation approaches have been implemented in the program M.
source: Similar tilt-series and CTF optimisation approaches have been implemented in the program M (Tegunov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with citation to M.

claim: Compared to M, RELION-4.0 uses computationally more efficient algorithms.
source: Compared to M, RELION-4.0 uses computationally more efficient algorithms; M uses GPUs to accelerate the calculations.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between RELION-4.0 and M.

claim: M uses GPUs to accelerate the calculations.
source: Compared to M, RELION-4.0 uses computationally more efficient algorithms; M uses GPUs to accelerate the calculations.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of M.

claim: In both tomography and SPA, RELION-4.0 only models beam-induced translations of the particles, whereas M also models beam-induced rotations.
source: In both tomography and SPA, RELION-4.0 only models beam-induced translations of the particles, whereas M also models beam-induced rotations.
evidence: This is stated as a difference between RELION-4.0 and M.

claim: SPA routinely reaches 2 Å resolutions without modelling beam-induced rotations.
source: Since SPA routinely reaches 2 Å resolutions without modelling beam-induced rotations, we assumed that the effect of rotations of individual particles throughout the tilt series is not large enough to warrant their correction at typical tomography resolutions.
evidence: This is stated as justification for not modeling rotations.

claim: The effect of rotations of individual particles throughout the tilt series is not large enough to warrant their correction at typical tomography resolutions.
source: Since SPA routinely reaches 2 Å resolutions without modelling beam-induced rotations, we assumed that the effect of rotations of individual particles throughout the tilt series is not large enough to warrant their correction at typical tomography resolutions.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption based on SPA experience.

claim: In cases where the data allow for better than 2 Å resolutions, M could still be used to correct for beam-induced rotations in a postprocessing step, following alignment and classification of the individual particles in RELION.
source: In cases where the data do allow for better than 2 Å resolutions, M could still be used to correct for beam-induced rotations in a postprocessing step, following alignment and classification of the individual particles in RELION.
evidence: This is stated as a potential workflow combining RELION and M.

claim: Adaptation of M to function with the pseudo-subtomograms proposed here would likely lead to increased synergy between the two programs.
source: It is likely that adaptation of M, in order to function with the pseudo-subtomograms proposed here, would lead to increased synergy between the two programs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future development.

claim: External tools to convert from M parameters to RELION-4.0 are already available.
source: In the meantime, external tools to convert from M parameters to RELION-4.0 are already available (https://github.com/joton/reliontomotools; Zivanov, 2022 copy archived at swh:1:rev:bfa43828876ceb77bed0c7eb72f794c79c9de5e6).
evidence: This is stated with a link to the tools.

claim: The uptake of the Bayesian approach by researchers new to the field is facilitated through the implementation of a graphical user interface.
source: Besides the reduction in tunable parameters that is characteristic of the Bayesian approach, its uptake by researchers that are new to the field is further facilitated through the implementation of a graphical user interface.
evidence: This is stated as a benefit of the GUI.

claim: The RELION interface is already widely used for single-particle analysis and has been extended for the processing of tomographic data in RELION-4.0.
source: This interface is already widely used for single-particle analysis and has been extended for the processing of tomographic data in RELION-4.0.
evidence: This describes the GUI extension.

claim: Tilt-series alignment, tomogram reconstruction, and particle picking are not yet part of the RELION workflow.
source: However, tilt-series alignment, tomogram reconstruction, and particle picking are not yet part of the RELION workflow.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation.

claim: Efforts to implement solutions for tilt-series alignment, tomogram reconstruction, and particle picking in a single tomography processing pipeline are ongoing and will be part of future RELION releases.
source: Efforts to also implement solutions for those steps in a single tomography processing pipeline are ongoing and will be part of future RELION releases.
evidence: This is stated as a future development plan.

claim: Current import procedures rely on specific preprocessing operations in IMOD.
source: Meanwhile, current import procedures rely on specific preprocessing operations in IMOD (Kremer et al., 1996), and particle coordinate conversion tools to use in RELION-4.0 are available for a range of third-party software packages (Pyle et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the current workflow with citations.

claim: Particle coordinate conversion tools to use in RELION-4.0 are available for a range of third-party software packages.
source: Meanwhile, current import procedures rely on specific preprocessing operations in IMOD (Kremer et al., 1996), and particle coordinate conversion tools to use in RELION-4.0 are available for a range of third-party software packages (Pyle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: An online tutorial using the publicly available HIV-1 immature capsid data set has been provided to describe and illustrate all steps necessary to obtain the results.
source: To further facilitate the uptake of this new software by the community, we have provided an online tutorial that uses the publicly available HIV-1 immature capsid data set to describe and illustrate all steps necessary to obtain the results described in Figure 1.
evidence: This describes the tutorial provided.

claim: The new methods for subtomogram averaging allow structure determination to resolutions that are sufficient for de novo atomic modelling.
source: In summary, we introduce new methods for subtomogram averaging to resolutions that are sufficient for de novo atomic modelling and increase the accessibility of this emerging technique.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the contribution.

claim: The new methods increase the accessibility of subtomogram averaging.
source: In summary, we introduce new methods for subtomogram averaging to resolutions that are sufficient for de novo atomic modelling and increase the accessibility of this emerging technique.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the contribution.

claim: The methods will allow more researchers to calculate better structures from tomographic data.
source: We envision that our methods will allow more researchers to calculate better structures from tomographic data, which will aid the next revolution in structural biology, where macromolecular complexes are imaged, not in isolation, but in their biologically relevant environment.
evidence: This is stated as an expected impact.

claim: The methods will aid the next revolution in structural biology, where macromolecular complexes are imaged in their biologically relevant environment rather than in isolation.
source: We envision that our methods will allow more researchers to calculate better structures from tomographic data, which will aid the next revolution in structural biology, where macromolecular complexes are imaged, not in isolation, but in their biologically relevant environment.
evidence: This is stated as a vision for the future of structural biology.
